stem: During long-term follow-up of a liver transplant recipient on maintenance corticosteroids, which complication should the coordinator include in surveillance teaching?

options.text: Metabolic bone disease, with greatest risk when steroid doses are highest
Metabolic bone disease never occurs after liver transplantation
Bone disease risk ends immediately when steroids are first prescribed
Only recipients under age 18 develop post-transplant bone disease

explanation.rationale_correct: Metabolic bone disease risk is greatest immediately after transplantation when steroid doses are highest, although some recipients remain at long-term risk even with lower or no steroid use.

rationale_incorrect.B: Metabolic bone disease is a recognized long-term complication after solid-organ transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Risk is highest early when steroid doses are highest rather than ending when steroids are initiated.
rationale_incorrect.D: Bone disease risk applies to transplant recipients broadly, not pediatric recipients alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 12, Long-Term Outcomes → E. Metabolic bone disease
primary_anchor.quote_hint: The greatest risk is immediately after transplantation when steroid doses are highest

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 12 → E. Metabolic bone disease (greatest risk when steroid doses highest; some long-term risk persists); PDF p. 674 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Seventh 030400 item; closes task gap; metabolic-bone angle distinct from skin cancer (cctc-3054), diabetes incidence (cctc-3028), and malignancy combo (cctc-3043); anchor verified on Cupples p. 674.

stem: When facilitating discharge medication teaching for a kidney recipient, which structured adherence strategy aligns with standard references?

options.text: A day-and-hour medication box that may be pre-loaded by the pharmacist at discharge
Storing all immunosuppressants in the bathroom medicine cabinet for convenience
Taking critical-dose drugs at random times without regard to drug-level draws
Avoiding any written medication roster because pictures are never helpful

explanation.rationale_correct: Structured medication management may include a medication box with day and hour subdivisions that can be pre-loaded by the pharmacist at discharge, along with a written roster and dosing reminders.

rationale_incorrect.B: Medications should not be stored in humid areas such as the bathroom; correct storage is part of discharge teaching.
rationale_incorrect.C: Critical-dose immunosuppressants must be taken at consistent times, especially around serum drug-level draws.
rationale_incorrect.D: A written medication roster with pictures, times, and doses supports accurate home dosing.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → medication education → structured approach
primary_anchor.quote_hint: medication box with day and hour subdivisions. The box may be pre-loaded by the pharmacist at the time of discharge

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → medication education → structured approach (day/hour medication box pre-loaded by pharmacist at discharge); PDF p. 107 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Seventh 030600 item; closes task gap; medication-box angle distinct from PPI–MMF interaction (cctc-3056), missed-dose teaching (cctc-3014), and grapefruit (cctc-3031); anchor verified on Cupples p. 107.

stem: A heart recipient preparing to return to employment after transplant asks about work re-entry. Which coordination counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Counsel the patient to initially telework or work part-time and gradually increase as energy improves
Require immediate return to full-time heavy labor without assessment
Permanent unemployment is expected for all transplant recipients
Return-to-work planning never considers job-specific restrictions

explanation.rationale_correct: Return-to-work counseling includes timing based on recovery and employment type, with initial telework or part-time work and gradual increase to full-time employment as energy improves, along with assessment of work activities for restrictions.

rationale_incorrect.B: Work re-entry is individualized and may begin with part-time or modified duties rather than immediate unrestricted heavy labor.
rationale_incorrect.C: Many recipients return to work with gradual progression rather than permanent unemployment.
rationale_incorrect.D: Work activities are assessed for suitability and potential restrictions such as weightlifting or toxic exposures.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → n. Return to work → ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Counsel patient to initially telework or work part-time (e.g., half days) and gradually increase to full-time employment as energy level improves

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → n. Return to work → ii. (initial telework/part-time with gradual return to full-time); PDF p. 121 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Eighth 030500 item; heart return-to-work angle distinct from day-after-discharge call (cctc-3055) and lymphocele monitoring (cctc-3052); anchor verified on Cupples p. 121.

stem: A lung recipient develops progressive airflow decline more than one year after transplant. Which chronic complication should the coordinator include in the differential?

options.text: Primary graft nonfunction occurring only in the first 72 hours
Hyperacute antibody-mediated rejection immediately at implantation only
Urinary leak near the kidney allograft

explanation.rationale_correct: Chronic lung allograft dysfunction includes bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS), a form of chronic rejection that limits long-term survival after lung transplantation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary graft dysfunction occurs within the first 72 hours, not as progressive chronic airflow decline a year later.
rationale_incorrect.C: Hyperacute rejection occurs immediately after implantation rather than as late progressive airflow decline.
rationale_incorrect.D: Urinary leak is a kidney surgical complication, not a chronic lung allograft process.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 11, Lung Transplantation → Monitor for Postoperative Complications → A.3.a.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 11 → Monitor for Postoperative Complications → A.3.a. (chronic rejection: bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome); PDF p. 607 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Ninth 030200 item; lung BOS chronic-rejection angle distinct from surgical wound infection (cctc-3050) and cholangitis (cctc-3039); anchor verified on Cupples p. 607.
